new_statements.quote: Haruna 2003 p.26: "Tone[.] Like all other Chadic languages, Gùrdùŋ is a tone language, i.e. each syllable in Gùrdùŋ has its own pitch, and this pitch is as much an essential element of that syllable as its consonant(s) and vowel(s). Gùrdùŋ has two basic tones - high (Hi) and low (Lo). Besides, there is a rising (Ri) tone (from Lo to Hi). Falling (Fa) tones (from Hi to Lo) are extremely rare. The tones are indicated by accents over the vowels ..." | p.17: "The suprasegmental level (tone): Tonal phonemes (tonemes) are a component of every syllable. Gùrdùŋ has two level tones: high (Hi) and low (Lo). Besides these two levels there is a rising (Ri) tone which must be considered a combination of Lo and Hi." | Hartmann & Zimmermann 2006 p.64 (saved PDF): "At the phonological level, Gùrùntùm is a tone language with two level tones H (´) and L (`), plus a falling (^) and (very rarely) a rising tone combination (Haruna 2003:26)."

new_statements.rule_in_words: Guruntum is described purely as a lexical tone language (H, L level tones on every syllable; rising contour = L+H, falling contour very rare; noun tone classes unpredictable). None of the accessible descriptions makes any statement about word stress/accent; H&Z 2006 explicitly note that no comprehensive study of the prosodic system exists.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. (Tonal notes only: rising tones typically before word-final sonorants, cf. Haruna 2003 p.27 fn.26; H&Z argue focus marker a is toneless and takes boundary L%.)
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is assigned per syllable (word-level lexical tone). Only phrase-level intonation facts mentioned are question intonation particles (Haruna 2003 sec. 8.8) and an L% boundary tone at the right edge of VP (H&Z 2006 sec. 5.3). The absence of a stress statement in Haruna 2003 is inferred from repeated zero-hit full-text snippet queries ('stress', 'stressed', 'accentuation', 'penultimate'), not from reading pp.17-30 in full.
new_statements.identity_note: Haruna 2003 describes Gùrdùŋ/Gùrùntùm proper (his informants mainly Gùrdùŋ-Kùukù dialect; he contrasts Gùrdùŋ-Gayar dialect features pp.10-11, incl. a 'Tone' dialect note 1.11.1.4). Hartmann & Zimmermann's speaker is also Gùrdùŋ-Kùukù. Glottolog guru1271 'Guruntum-Mbaaru' [grd] covers the Guruntum-Mbaaru complex; the Mbaaru variety is not separately described in any source seen.

Sec. 5.3: 'a comprehensive study of the prosodic system of Gùrùntùm is still lacking'; discusses boundary tones (L%) and toneless focus marker a; nothing on word stress. Own fieldwork with a Gùrdùŋ-Kùukù dialect speaker.
